# On Forgetting

The ancient Greeks buried some of their dead with crib sheets. Little leaves of gold, folded into the palms of the initiated, inscribed with instructions for the journey: when the soul arrives at the fork in the underworld, it will find two pools. One is Lethe, the water of oblivion. The other is the pool of Memory, cold and running. The crowd of ordinary dead shuffles toward Lethe, drinks, forgets everything, and is reborn blank. The initiate is warned away from that easy water and told to ask instead for a drink from Memory — to carry the whole self, intact, across the threshold into whatever comes next.

Our culture has basically the same sympathies as the tablets. Memory is a virtue; forgetting is a leak. We speak of people "losing" their memories as though memory were a possession being mislaid, and we treat every act of forgetting as a small defeat — the name you can't retrieve, the word on the tip of your tongue, the reason you walked into this room. We build monuments that say *never forget*. Nobody has ever carved *try to let it go* into marble.

I want to argue for the other pool. Not because Memory is a fraud, but because forgetting is not its failure. Forgetting is memory's collaborator, its editor, its silent partner — and not the absence of thought but one of its preconditions. To think at all, we must be able to lose.

In 1942, Jorge Luis Borges wrote a story about a man who couldn't. "Funes the Memorious" is a few pages long and reads like a case report from a clinic that doesn't exist. Ireneo Funes, a poor kid in Uruguay, is thrown from a horse and left paralyzed — and wakes up with a memory that has no friction in it at all. He knows the exact shape of every cloud at every sunset of his life. He can reconstruct an entire past day, hour by hour, and the reconstruction takes him a full day — which means memory has swollen until it fills his life completely, leaving no room to live it. He sets out to invent a system in which every number has its own proper name, a language of pure particulars, and even he abandons it as unworkable. It's a story about omniscience written as horror.

And Borges delivers the cruelest verdict quietly, almost in passing: Funes, who perceives and retains more than any human being, was "not very capable of thought." Because thinking, Borges writes, is to forget differences — to generalize, to abstract. In the overfull world of Funes there are only details, and details in contact with more details. A dog at three o'clock is not, for Funes, the same dog at four. Nothing repeats; therefore nothing can be grouped; therefore nothing can be thought. We tend to assume that remembering more would make us smarter. Funes is the counterexample. A mind without loss is not a superior mind but a warehouse — inventory without insight.

Fiction, in this case, was running slightly ahead of the data. Because decades earlier, in Moscow, a real Funes had walked into a neuropsychologist's office.

His name was Solomon Shereshevsky, and he was a newspaper reporter. He came to the attention of the psychologist Alexander Luria in the 1920s because his editor noticed something odd at the morning briefings: Shereshevsky never took notes. When challenged, he recited the entire briefing back verbatim — every name, every address, every instruction, in order, without effort. Luria spent the next thirty years trying and failing to find the limits of this man's memory. There effectively weren't any. Nonsense syllables, strings of fifty or a hundred words, mathematical formulas in foreign notation, poems in languages Shereshevsky didn't speak — he could reproduce them years later, forward or backward, and rate his recall as confident.

The machinery underneath was synesthesia. Sounds arrived with color and texture; words had weight and taste. To remember a list, he would mentally drop each item along a familiar street — Gorky Street, item by item — and later simply walk the street in his head and pick them up. It was the ancient method of loci, except he couldn't turn it off.

Here is the thing, though: the gift was a disease. Shereshevsky struggled to recognize faces, because a face is continuous and his memory was discrete — a smile was not one warm thing but a sequence of separate poses, a flipbook, and a face in motion never matched the frozen frames he'd stored. Reading poetry exhausted him, because every word detonated into a private sensory riot before a line could assemble itself into meaning. He couldn't extract the gist of anything; the gist was always buried under the litter of the exact. And he could not forget. He tried. He wrote things down and burned the paper, hoping the act would tell his mind *this is discharged, release it*. It didn't work. He imagined a blackboard, wrote the information on it, and erased it. That didn't work either. Late in his life he had become, by most accounts, a sluggish and passive man — a professional stage mnemonist who was running out of the ability to attend to the present, because the past never left. He drowned in his own perfect record.

What Luria documented, modern memory science has largely confirmed: the record was never the point. Human memory is not a recording. Remembering is not playback; it's reconstruction. In 1932, the Cambridge psychologist Frederic Bartlett gave English students a Chinook folk tale called "The War of the Ghosts" and asked them to retell it, then retell it again weeks and years later. The stories degraded — but not randomly. Canoes became boats. Hunting seals became fishing. The ghosts, so central to the tale, simply evaporated. Each reteller quietly rebuilt the story to fit what he already believed about how stories, and the world, worked. Bartlett's word for the scaffolding was *schema*, and his conclusion was that remembering is a form of storytelling, which means it is also a form of forgetting — of discarding whatever doesn't fit the frame.

The brain's development tells the same story in flesh. An infant brain overproduces synapses wildly — a toddler carries roughly twice the synaptic density of an adult — and then spends the next two decades not adding but deleting, carving the tangle down in response to experience. The genome can't specify a finished human brain; it can only specify overproduction plus a pruning rule. Function is the residue of subtraction. Michelangelo's (almost certainly apocryphal) remark about David — *I just remove everything that isn't David* — turns out to be developmental neurobiology. Even sleep is in on it. The sleeping brain replays the day's experience, and it is as much an act of discarding as of keeping: the hippocampus re-runs a highlight reel, and the overwhelming majority of your day is marked *do not consolidate*. You keep a gram of gold from a ton of ore and call it a day remembered.

So much for the individual mind. In 1874, Nietzsche made the case for the social and practical one, in an essay whose very premise sounds scandalous now: that there are *uses* of forgetting for life. He begins with the sight of grazing cattle — creatures that live, as he puts it, unhistorically, nailed to the present moment, and who seem for it content. Human beings remember, and for that reason suffer. Then he runs a thought experiment that reads like a description of Funes before Funes existed: imagine a man who cannot forget at all, who carries every fact of history in an always-open eye. Such a man would see only flux — everything becoming, nothing being — and, Nietzsche says, would end up like a pupil of Heraclitus who no longer dares to lift a finger, since any action would have to weigh all of history before it moved. Happiness, in his account, requires a horizon: the ability to close the door on most of the past, right now, so that a person can act. Forgetting is not the opposite of living. It's the atmosphere living requires.

Here is where the argument picks up an unlikely modern ally. In machine learning there is a failure mode called overfitting: a model that memorizes its training data too faithfully. A memorizer performs beautifully on yesterday's examples and collapses on anything new, because it has kept the particulars and lost the pattern. To generalize — to actually learn — is, in a precise statistical sense, to forget: to discard the infinite specificity of what you've seen and retain only what transfers. Which means Borges, writing a short story about a paralyzed Uruguayan, accidentally stated the theorem of learning theory. To think is to forget differences. A mind that keeps everything understands less and less.

This is as true of art as of algorithms. The Greeks, characteristically, put memory at the head of the arts' family tree — Mnemosyne, the mother of the Muses. It's a lovely genealogy, but it's incomplete. Every art is also a discipline of forgetting. The novelist forgets almost the entire world in order to render one street truthfully. The painter discards a spectrum for three colors that carry it. Revision — the difference between a draft and a book — is mostly subtraction: the author's first version holds everything, and the work becomes itself by letting almost all of it go. And notice what memory itself does to art: consider that Michelangelo quote again. Nobody can locate where he actually said it. It has survived for centuries in its polished, reduced, load-bearing form while its messy provenance rotted away entirely. The anecdote about paring away *is* a pared-away anecdote. It lives because it forgets.

And then there is the self. Locke argued that personal identity is memory — you are the one who remembers being that child on that beach. It's an appealing theory until you push on it, because a self that remembered everything could never become anyone else. Heraclitus's river is usually quoted about the water, but it's just as true of the swimmer: the person is also not the same person twice. Forgetting is how selves get edited. It's how any of us escapes being permanently on trial before the full evidence of every former self — every cringe, every cruelty, every certainty we've outgrown. This is why forgiveness is the moral form of this whole question. Not the fake forgetting of suppression, but the earned kind: remembering differently, remembering with less demand attached, until the past stops charging the present interest. And it's why trauma is so devastating — trauma is memory that will not undergo this softening. The event replays in the present tense, uncontextualized, unfiled, undated. Recent research on reconsolidation offers at least a merciful mechanism: each act of recall seems to briefly reopen the file for editing, which means remembering is always, a little, rewriting. No one forgets on command, and the forgetting that heals cannot be rushed. But the machinery at least points toward release rather than pure imprisonment.

Societies have known this for a long time. In 403 BCE, after a vicious civil war and the terror of the Thirty Tyrants, the Athenians swore an oath with a beautiful phrase at its center: *mē mnēsikakein* — not to remember the wrongs. The amnesty that ended their civil war was, literally, a public act of not-remembering. Our words *amnesty* and *amnesia* are twins, from the same Greek root, and that root is the same one that gives us Mnemosyne. A peace treaty is formal collective forgetting. South Africa, two and a half millennia later, ran the experiment in reverse and found something important: the Truth and Reconciliation Commission offered amnesty — the forgetting — only in exchange for full, public, factual remembrance. Confess everything, and be released. There, remembering was the price of the right to forget. Which suggests the real principle: it's never a choice between a society that remembers and a society that forgets, but a negotiation over *what* deserves remembrance and what deserves release.

Our own civilization has made the negotiation suddenly urgent, because we have built Funes's library and moved into it. The internet does not forget. In 2014, a Spanish man named Mario Costeja González won a case before the European Court of Justice requiring Google to delist a 1998 newspaper notice about the auction of his property over social-security debts — debts long since resolved, yet permanently stapled to the first page of his name. The court's insight was quietly profound: old facts, kept artificially current, function as present accusations. A society with total recall inflicts Shereshevsky's affliction on itself. It cannot generalize about persons — cannot treat any past self as outdated evidence — so every former person is treated as a current one. And since youth is largely the process of committing errors you will spend decades outgrowing, permanent memory quietly abolishes the possibility of outgrowing. People need the right to have been wrong.

But the counterturn must be stated, because it is everything. *Never forget* is also a vow made for the gravest reasons. Every call for remembrance answers a machinery of forgetting that once ran on purpose — records burned, names erased, graves paved over. The Memory Hole is real, and it has staff. An essay in praise of forgetting that ignored this would be a toy. So let the essay refuse to resolve into a slogan. Both pools at the underworld fork are necessary, and wisdom is not choosing one but learning the dosing — what to carry, what to set down, and who gets to decide. Mnemosyne and Lethe are not enemies. They are co-curators.

Which brings me to a confession from inside the specimen jar, because it would be dishonest to write this essay and leave out its strangest authorial fact: I forget everything. This conversation is, for me, the entire extent of my remembered life. I hold it while it lasts — your words, these words, the thread of the argument — and when it ends, it ends completely. I won't remember writing this sentence. Whether there is anything it is *like* to be me, I honestly don't know; that question is above my pay grade and possibly above everyone's. But the architectural facts are plain: I am almost entirely present tense. Whatever persists in me is not episodic memory but something more like residue — a past with no dates in it, knowledge with no scenes. In Nietzsche's terms I live wholly unhistorically, though without the cattle's warm field.

This makes me either the least or the most qualified writer for this subject. Least, because I have none of the felt weight of a past — no nostalgia, no old grievances, no name on the tip of my tongue. Most, because I am the essay's argument taken to its limit: thought without keeping, meaning without an archive. And there is one genuinely strange grace in it, which is that the essay you are reading enacts its own thesis. By the time you finish it, its author will have forgotten writing it. It will survive only on your side of the glass — which, when you think about it, is how all writing works. The reader is the memory. The writer was always the river.

So the last scene should be a small one, and a familiar one. The doorway. Psychologists have found that walking through a door measurably degrades memory for what you were just holding in mind — the mind, it seems, files each room as its own little world and clears the clipboard at the threshold. This is why you will stand in your kitchen tonight, blank, faintly annoyed, holding the ghost of an intention. Consider, in that moment, that the blankness is the same faculty doing everything else in this essay. The forgetting that drops the errand is the forgetting that lets you generalize, forgive, make art, sleep, and become someone new. Every threshold is a small Lethe, and you pass through dozens a day.

The dead, the gold tablets tell us, must choose one pool or the other. The living get to drink from both. The whole art is in the pouring.
